title: Contains is law. May contain is not.
standfirst: One of these lines is required. The other one is a choice.

spans.text: A label can talk about an allergen in more than one way, and those ways do not carry the same weight. Knowing which one you are reading changes what it tells you.

If a maker puts one of the major allergens in a food on purpose, US law makes them name it in plain words. That is the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act, and the FASTER Act later added sesame to the list.
The EU has its own version, and it works the same way: a named ingredient, in the ingredient list, in a form you can find.
So "contains milk" is a fact a maker is obliged to tell you. You can lean on it.
The line that is a choice

"May contain milk" is different. Nobody requires it, nobody defines it, and nobody checks it. A maker adds it when they think there is a chance of cross contact — flour dust in the air, a shared line, a shared blade.
Because it is voluntary, its absence tells you nothing at all. A food with no warning may still be made on a shared line. A food with a warning may never have touched the allergen.
The warning is about the factory, not the recipe. It is a maker telling you what they are unsure of, in words they chose themselves.
What this means when you are standing in the aisle
Read the ingredient list first, because that is the part the law governs. Read the warning second, and read it as a maker's judgement rather than a measurement.

There is no agreed threshold behind a precautionary warning, so different makers can look at the same risk and label it differently. We can tell you what a label says. We cannot tell you what it left out.

We read both lines. When the ingredient list names an allergen you have told us to watch, we say so plainly. When only the voluntary warning mentions it, we say that too, in different words, because they are not the same claim.
On this one thing we would rather be wrong in the direction of caution than quiet.
